passages.happening:
“Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent” (verse 1).

Abraham looks up and sees “three men standing nearby”. He runs to meet them and bows to the ground (verse 2). “My lord,” he says, “if I have found favor in your sight, please do not pass your servant by” (verse 3). He offers a little water to wash their feet, rest under the tree, and “a bit of bread” (verses 4-5).

Then he hurries. He tells Sarah to bake bread from “three seahs of fine flour” (verse 6). He runs to the herd and chooses “a tender and choice calf” (verse 7). He serves them curds, milk and the calf, “and stood by them under the tree as they ate” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The heat of the day is the hour when no one moves. Abraham is an old man. Yet he runs, twice.

In the ancient world a stranger on the road was in real danger, with no family nearby to protect him. Hospitality turned a stranger into a protected guest: water for the feet, food, shelter and safety, at the host's own cost. A household's honor depended on it.

Abraham follows the polite form. He promises a little and gives a great deal. ‘A bit of bread’ becomes a feast. Three seahs of flour is a very large amount, far more than three guests could eat. Meat was rarely eaten and marked a special day. And Abraham does not sit with them. He stands by, like a servant in his own camp.

Who are the visitors? The text shifts as it goes. Verse 1 says the LORD appeared. Verse 2 says three men. Abraham speaks to them as ‘my lord’, then they answer together. Later the LORD speaks (verses 10 and 13), two of the men go on toward Sodom, and Abraham stays standing before the LORD (verse 22). In the next chapter the two are called angels (19:1). The reader learns step by step what Abraham did not know when he ran: he was welcoming the LORD.

The place was remembered for centuries. In the time of King Herod a large stone wall was built around the traditional site of Mamre, north of Hebron, and the emperor Constantine had a church built there in the 300s AD. That does not prove where the oaks stood, but it shows how long this meeting was honored.
passages.later:
Hebrews has this story in mind: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).

Jesus says that at the judgment the King will say, “I was a stranger and you took Me in” (Matthew 25:35). Welcoming the stranger is welcoming him.

The next chapter shows the opposite. When the two angels reach Sodom, the men of the city try to attack Lot's guests (Genesis 19). What Abraham does in the open field, the city refuses to do.
passages.hard:
Who were the three? Readers have answered in more than one way.

Many Jewish and Christian readers say that the LORD came with two angels, as the next chapter suggests (19:1). One of the three speaks for God, and the other two go on to Sodom.

Many Christians, especially in Eastern Orthodox churches, have seen in the three visitors a hint of the Trinity: one God in three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Andrei Rublev's famous Russian icon of the early fifteenth century, often called the Trinity, paints the three visitors at Abraham's table as a picture of that mystery. Some Christians also see in the one who speaks as the LORD an appearance of the Son before he was born as a man.

The text itself does not explain. It moves between ‘the LORD’ and ‘three men’ and lets the reader feel the mystery. The New Testament does not use this story to teach the Trinity. These notes take no side among these readings. All of them agree that God came near to Abraham as a guest at his table.
passages.asks: Abraham ran to welcome strangers, and found that God was among them. Ask who the strangers are near you: a new neighbor, a lonely person at church, someone who does not speak your language. Then ask what it would cost you to run to meet them.

passages.happening:
The visitors ask, “Where is your wife Sarah?” “There, in the tent,” he replies (verse 9).

The LORD says, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” Sarah is listening behind him at the tent door (verse 10). Both of them are old, and Sarah is long past the age of having children (verse 11).

“So she laughed to herself” and said, “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” (verse 12).

The LORD asks Abraham why Sarah laughed. “Is anything too difficult for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you” (verse 14). Sarah is afraid and says, “I did not laugh.” “No,” replied the LORD, “but you did laugh” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Sarah has heard nothing of the promises before this, as far as the story tells. Now she hears it from behind the tent door.

Her laugh is not cruel. It is the laugh of a woman who has waited for decades and has given up. She calls herself ‘worn out’. Her husband is old. The longing she buried years ago is suddenly stirred up again, and she laughs to keep from hoping.

The visitor knows she laughed, though she laughed to herself. That tells Abraham and Sarah who this guest is.

The question ‘Is anything too difficult for the LORD?’ is not a scolding. It is an invitation. Sarah is afraid and says she did not laugh. The LORD does not let the lie stand, but he does not take back the promise either. He gently insists: you did laugh. Her laugh is not the end of the story. A year later she will laugh again, for joy (21:6).
passages.later:
When the angel tells Mary that her old relative Elizabeth is pregnant, he says, “For no word from God will ever fail” (Luke 1:37). Many readers hear an echo of this chapter. The God who gave a son to Sarah gives a son to Elizabeth, and to Mary.

Jeremiah prays, “Nothing is too difficult for You” (Jeremiah 32:17). Hebrews says of Sarah that “she considered Him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11).
passages.hard:
A word of care. Sarah's story ends in joy, with a son in her old age. But that does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.

‘Is anything too difficult for the LORD?’ is true. It is not a promise that God will always do the thing we ask. It is a promise that our limits are not his limits, and that nothing we suffer is beyond his care.
passages.asks: Sarah laughed because she had stopped hoping, and then she was afraid to admit it. Ask where you have stopped hoping, and laughed it off. Then hear the question God asked her: ‘Is anything too difficult for the LORD?’

passages.t: ‘Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?’
passages.happening:
The men get up to leave and look out over Sodom. Abraham walks with them to see them off (verse 16).

The LORD says, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?” (verse 17). Abraham will become a great nation, “and through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed” (verse 18). God has chosen him “so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just” (verse 19).

Then the LORD says, “The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great. Because their sin is so grievous, I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
God speaks to himself, and the reader overhears. He decides to tell Abraham his plans, the way a person tells a friend.

The reason is in verse 19. Abraham's family is to be known for doing ‘what is right and just’. If Abraham is going to teach his children about God's justice, he needs to see it up close, and to ask about it.

‘Outcry’ is a strong word. In the Bible it is often the cry of people who are being wronged and calling for help. Something terrible is happening in Sodom, and the cries have reached God.

‘I will go down to see’ does not mean God does not know. Genesis uses the same picture at Babel (11:5). It shows God as a fair judge who looks carefully before he acts, so that no one can say he judged on rumor.
passages.later:
Israel's prophets later name the sins of Sodom. Ezekiel says, “She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). The next chapter of Genesis shows the city's violence toward strangers.

James calls Abraham “a friend of God” (James 2:23). And Jesus says to his disciples, “I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). A friend is told what the master is doing.
passages.asks: God told Abraham his plans so that Abraham would learn to care about justice. Ask what cries for help have reached you: in your town, your school, the news. Then ask whether you have brought them to God, or only scrolled past them.

passages.happening:
Two of the men turn toward Sodom, “but Abraham remained standing before the LORD” (verse 22).

Abraham steps forward: “Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” (verse 23). What if there are fifty righteous people in the city (verse 24)? “Far be it from You! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (verse 25).

The LORD says he will spare the whole city for fifty (verse 26). Abraham speaks again, calling himself “dust and ashes” (verse 27). Forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Each time the LORD agrees (verses 28-31). At last Abraham asks, “Suppose ten are found there?” And the LORD answers, “On account of the ten, I will not destroy it” (verse 32).

The LORD goes on his way, and Abraham returns home (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the first long prayers in the Bible, and it is an argument. Abraham does not simply accept what God says. He stands in God's way and pleads, and he bases his plea on God's own character: the Judge of all the earth must do what is right.

He is bold and humble at once. He calls himself ‘dust and ashes’. He keeps asking whether God will be angry. But he keeps asking.

It can sound like bargaining, but it is not haggling over a price. Abraham is asking how much mercy God will show. Each time, God says yes. He never says no. It is Abraham who stops at ten.

Abraham's nephew Lot lives in Sodom. Abraham must have had him in mind. But he does not pray only for Lot. He prays for the whole city.
passages.later:
Moses later pleads with God for Israel in the same bold way, and “the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people” (Exodus 32:14). God looks for someone to “stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land” (Ezekiel 22:30).

James says, “The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (James 5:16). Jesus told a parable “about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

The New Testament says that Christ “always lives to intercede” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). To intercede means to plead for someone else. Abraham asked that the righteous not die with the wicked. The gospel goes further: “Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18).
passages.hard:
Did Abraham change God's mind? Christians answer in more than one way.

Many hold that God knows the end from the beginning and does not change, and that prayer is one of the ways he has chosen to carry out his plans. Abraham's pleading was real, and it was also what God drew out of him by telling him his plan (verse 17). Others give more weight to the give-and-take of the conversation, and see a God who truly responds to those who pray. Both agree that God invites his people to plead with him, and that he is more merciful than Abraham dared to ask. These notes do not settle it.

What the story does settle is that prayer can be an argument. Abraham stood before God and pressed: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (verse 25). God did not rebuke the question. He let Abraham press it again and again. People of faith are allowed to bring their hardest questions about God's justice to God himself.
passages.asks: Abraham argued with God for a city that was not his own, on the ground of God's own goodness. Ask whom you have stopped praying for because they seem too far gone. Then ask what it would look like to stand before God for them, boldly and humbly, the way Abraham did.
